newsitem.title: UK: Global LPG strongest in Europe, steady elsewhere.
newsitem.headline: Global LPG strongest in Europe, steady elsewhere.

text.p: European propane prices continued rising throughout the week to Friday, while US levels fluctuated on mixed signals and the Far Eastern market slowed down on lack of interest at current high levels.
But butane prices have weakened, driven by different fundamantals, and a huge price differential is emerging between the two grades of Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG).

European propane prices have been rising inexorably for weeks, and this week the landmark $400 a tonne level was breached for large cif cargoes. "These are exciting times", said a Scandinavian trader whose company sold a 5,000 tonne piece at $410 cif northwest Europe earlier in the week.

He added that offer levels are even higher now, and felt that $420 a tonne may be achievable before 18 January, after which some storage facilites will be replenished and demand is expected to slow down.

The price is being sustained partly because, although European price levels are considerably higher than in other markets, there are logistical reasons why cargoes are not being moved in from elsewhere.

On the US Gulf Coast, shipping is not available immediately and when it is, there will have to be a delay before loading to allow the product to be cooled. This raises the possibility that the cargo would arrive too late, when European prices may have started to fall, and so far has prevented transatlantic movement from starting.
And from the Middle East, the length of the journey also seems to be ruling out sales into Europe, as no cargoes could now arrive before February, and the risk of lower prices then is a deterrent.

But Algerian Sonatrach is looking into the possibility of moving propane north. A trader at Sonatrach in London said the company is contemplating this action, but will take a few days to decide whether to go ahead. The Mediterranean market is quiet compared with the north, with large propane cargoes valued at around $380 a tonne cif Lavera, some $30 a tonne below north west Europe levels.

In the north, barge prices have reached $440 a tonne, with railcars even higher. And with a butane barge traded yesterday at $234.50 a tonne, the price differential between the two products has ballooned to over $200 a tonne.
The butane price is influenced by blending economics, rather than the weather and heating demand, and has become completely detached from the propane price in recent weeks.
In the US, propane levels have swung on weather and stock data. The week started strongly but prices dropped as EIA data showed an 800,000 barrel stock build in the week to January 3.
A return to cold weather sent prices up again as traders concluded that cold weather was more fundamentally important than apparently bearish inventory levels.

In the Middle East and Far East, premiums have fallen as the Saudi CP for January is considered high, too high for recent premiums to hold. Japanese buyers are bidding no more than CP +$30 a tonne now, a Japanese trader said, and he added that sellers are not far above this level. But the market is quiet. "Due to lack of requirements, no deals have been seen", said a trader.

Chinese demand is also still very slow, dealers said. There had been hopes that demand would pick up ahead of the lunar New Year in early February and provide a focus to all markets in east Asia. But this has so far failed to materialise and all markets in the region have been thin.

Falling premiums to the Saudi CP have opened a differential of up to $50 a tonne between propane cargoes on a c+f Japan basis and cargoes sold cif north west Europe. But the markets are different as few ports in Europe can handle the large cargoes that Japanese ports routinely handle.

Premiums for loading spot cargoes in the Gulf have also come down in reaction to the high Saudi CP. Many now expect the February CP to come down below January's level, but until it does, premiums are slipping instead.

Propane is now talked at around CP +$5 a tonne fob Gulf, with butane nearer CP +$10, but trade has been limited. The T1 tender for february was due to close on Friday, dealers said, and some were expecting the price to be similar to the last January tender, thought sold at around $340 a tonne fob Gulf.
